subtype: Approach: taking any offer without thinking [Pitfall]
passage:
“You look awful,” Eshaan said, dropping his bag next to Sarika in the corridor.
“Two nights. Don't start.”
“Two nights of what?”
“Deliveries. After ten. A man from a group chat offered it, no forms, no questions. Easy money.”
“And the maths test you slept through?”
“It's one test.”
“What was in the bags?”
Sarika looked at the floor. “He said not to open them.”
“Did he pay you?”
“Friday. He promised.”
“Last night, what happened?”
“A car kept slowing beside me. I dumped the bags at the tea stall and ran.” Her hands were shaking now.
“Then he's not paying you Friday. Come on, we're telling the counsellor. Right now.”
Sarika nodded. At the office the counsellor looked up, saw her face and said, “Sit down. You're not in trouble.”

qa.q: How many nights had Sarika delivered bags?
qa.a: Two nights.

qa.q: What might Sarika be feeling as she describes the car?
qa.a: Fear: her hands are shaking as she admits she ran, which shows the easy money no longer feels safe.

qa.q: What should Sarika have done before accepting, and why?
qa.a: She should have asked who the man was, what was in the bags and the exact hours, and told a parent or teacher first, because vague terms and night work for a school student are warning signs.

qa.q: How does the job look to Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan sees a stranger handing a schoolmate unknown bags at night, so he worries about her safety and wants a trusted adult involved straight away.

grounding: A student takes a night delivery job with vague terms, and it proves unsafe and clashes with school.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable version of a small business [Action]
passage:
Aparna: Made ten Diwali cards last night! Marigolds and little diyas 🙂
Lalremsiami: Only ten? Why not fifty?
Aparna: Paper and paint cost money. If nobody buys, I'm stuck with forty. Ten first.
Lalremsiami: Fair. Who's buying?
Aparna: Relatives, neighbours, Sir at tuition. I'll carry them in a folder.
(two days later)
Aparna: Sold eight! Two aunts, three neighbours, Sir bought one for his mother.
Lalremsiami: Nice!! So make more?
Aparna: Two cousins asked for Bhai Dooj ones. Nobody wanted the star ones. So twenty-five more, only diya and Bhai Dooj designs.
Lalremsiami: Smart. Save me one 😊

qa.q: How many cards did Aparna sell in two days?
qa.a: Eight cards.

qa.q: What might Aparna be feeling about the sales?
qa.a: Encouraged and cautiously excited: eight cards sold, and the plan for more is based on which designs people actually asked for.

qa.q: What else could Aparna do to learn from buyers, and why?
qa.a: Ask each buyer which card they liked best and what they would pay, because direct answers cost nothing and guide the next batch.

qa.q: How might a neighbour who bought a card see Aparna's plan?
qa.a: A neighbour gets an affordable handmade gift and the pleasure of supporting a local student, and their choice of design helps Aparna decide what to make.

grounding: A student makes ten cards, sells them to relatives and neighbours and uses the response to decide about making more.

subtype: Approach: pricing by costs and time [Thinking]
passage: “Shalini, you asked how I picked my bookmark price, so here's the honest version. At first I charged ten rupees because everyone smiled and said ‘so cheap!’ Then one night I counted. Card, thread and glue came to about six rupees each, and every bookmark took twenty minutes. Ten minus six is four rupees for twenty minutes. That's twelve rupees an hour, if I'm lucky. I looked at what the stationery shop and the lady next door charged for similar ones, twenty-five to thirty-five. So I set thirty. Two people grumbled. My stomach did a little flip. But I could keep making them, and I finally understood that pricing low to please everyone meant I'd quit by Diwali. I'm Alka, by the way.”

qa.q: How many minutes did each bookmark take?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Alka feel on realising the ten-rupee price left so little?
qa.a: Worry mixed with sober clarity: Alka saw that pleasing buyers with a tiny price would end in giving up.

qa.q: What could Alka try if two buyers still grumble, and why?
qa.a: Alka could offer a set of bookmarks at a bundle price or a simpler design at a lower price, since that keeps costs and time covered while giving buyers a choice.

qa.q: How might a buyer used to the ten-rupee price see the change?
qa.a: A buyer may be surprised at first, but seeing the price match neighbours' similar work and the effort involved could make it feel fair.

grounding: A student adds material costs and time, compares with neighbours, and sets a fair price after seeing that underpricing is unsustainable.

passage: By October Damini had twelve small students on the veranda in three batches, from four in the afternoon till nine at night. The first fee money had made her giddy, and every new child felt like another win. The steel tin behind the rice sack grew heavy. But her own homework was done on the bus, half-copied, and she slept five hours. In the monthly test her maths marks fell from sixty-eight to forty-one. “Your notebook's empty,” her friend Ira said at lunch. Damini snapped that she was earning. That night she sat with the marked test in one hand and the tin in the other, counting both. The rupees suddenly looked small beside everything they had cost.

qa.q: How many students did Damini have by October?
qa.a: Twelve, in three batches.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when Ira said the notebook was empty?
qa.a: Defensive and stung: she snapped that she was earning, though the falling marks were already worrying her.

qa.q: What could Damini do instead, and why might it work?
qa.a: She could keep only a few students on fixed evenings and protect sleep and homework time, because steady marks and rest matter more than extra money.

qa.q: How might Ira see Damini's plan?
qa.a: Ira sees a friend who is tired, short-tempered and behind on homework, and worries that the tutoring is costing more than it earns.

grounding: Excited by early earnings, a student takes on many tutees, and homework, sleep and marks suffer.

subtype: Approach: buffer and weekly hour cap [Revision]
passage: At the parent-teacher meeting, Sunaina ma'am slid Baljeet's report across the desk: science down twelve marks. Baljeet's father had come along and folded his arms. Baljeet had brought a page. “Six hours a week, Saturday mornings at the print shop, nothing more. No work at all in February and March, the board months. If marks drop again, Papa can pause it, no arguing.” Papa read the page twice. “Why six?” “Because last month I did fourteen and fell asleep in class.” Sunaina ma'am nodded and suggested they look at the numbers again after the next test. Papa took out a pen and signed the page under Baljeet's name.

qa.q: How many hours a week did Baljeet cap the work at?
qa.a: Six hours.

qa.q: What might Baljeet be feeling while handing Papa the page?
qa.a: Nervous but determined: Baljeet prepared a plan in advance and even invites Papa to pause the job, which shows a wish to win back trust.

qa.q: What else could help Baljeet protect study time, and why?
qa.a: A fixed study slot before each work shift, since it puts homework first instead of leaving it for whatever time is left.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Papa?
qa.a: Papa, who watched the marks fall, may feel relieved that Baljeet has set a limit and given him a way to step in without a quarrel.

grounding: After a dip in marks, a student caps work hours, blocks the exam months and agrees with the parents when to pause.

passage: Jaya's first month of Saturday tutoring brought in twelve hundred rupees, and the festival sale began in two days. Her brother Lokesh waved a flyer. “Spend half now, you've earned it!” Jaya took her school notebook and ruled three columns: Home, Laptop, Mine. Four hundred for Amma's household jar, five hundred toward the laptop, three hundred to spend. She wrote each amount and the date. “Only three hundred?” Lokesh groaned. “Three hundred, and I choose how,” Jaya said, and bought a sketch pad for two hundred and fifty, putting fifty back. At night she totted up the columns again. The laptop column looked tiny beside the price she'd seen online, but next to last month's zero it was a start.

qa.q: How much did Jaya set aside toward the laptop?
qa.a: Five hundred rupees.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel looking at the laptop column that night?
qa.a: A little proud but slightly disappointed: it looked small beside the laptop's price yet bigger than last month's nothing.

qa.q: What else could Jaya add to the notebook, and why?
qa.a: A target amount and month for the laptop, since knowing how many months it will take makes the saving feel real and planned.

qa.q: How does the split look to Amma?
qa.a: Amma sees that Jaya's contribution to the household comes first, and may feel proud that Jaya is planning with real money.

grounding: A student splits earnings into family, savings and spending and records them in a notebook, learning to budget.

subtype: Approach: learning from an unhappy customer [Revision]
passage: In her bedroom in Melbourne, Aiko packed the last of the week's orders: hand-sewn bag charms she sold through a small online shop. Then Layla's message arrived: “I ordered this for my sister's birthday on Saturday. It came on Monday. She had already had her party.” Aiko's stomach dropped. She had said Thursday, and it had taken eight days because she'd been at a school trip. She wrote back: “I'm so sorry. You're right, and I promised something I couldn't keep. I'll remake it in the colour you wanted and post it today, free.” Layla replied with a photo of the new charm on a school bag and a smile. Aiko rewrote her shop page: every date now had two extra days added, and she kept the message pinned above her desk.

qa.q: What did Aiko change about the delivery dates she gives?
qa.a: She added two extra days to every date.

qa.q: How did Aiko feel when Layla's message arrived, and afterwards?
qa.a: Sad and embarrassed at first, then happy and relieved once Layla sent a photo of the new charm.

qa.q: What else could Aiko do to prevent late orders, and why?
qa.a: She could post her current making time on the shop page, so buyers choose with realistic timing and fewer disappointments.

qa.q: How does the late order look to Layla?
qa.a: Layla counted on the promised date for a birthday, so missing it feels like a broken promise, though a quick apology and a remake can restore some trust.

grounding: A student apologises for a late order, redoes the work and starts promising realistic dates, treating feedback as a cheap way to learn.

subtype: Approach: reflecting on whether the gig fits long-term goals [Revision]
passage: I'm Vasudha, Hemant's older sister, and I watched him do something odd last Sunday. He spread three months of gig notes across the floor: a price spreadsheet for the tailor, a poster for the bakery, a small website for his tuition class, folding flyers, updating a shop's phone list. Next to each he drew a tick or a question mark. Ticks went beside the spreadsheet and the website. “What will this teach me for college?” he muttered. He crossed out the flyers and the phone list. “Coding first, maybe the poster,” he told me. I don't know whether he was sad to lose the small money, since he went quiet for a while, but then he opened his laptop and messaged the tuition teacher asking for another site to build.

qa.q: Which tasks did Hemant cross out?
qa.a: The flyers and the phone list.

qa.q: What might Hemant have been feeling when he went quiet after crossing out the small jobs?
qa.a: Some regret at losing the small money, mixed with determination, since he then asked for more coding work.

qa.q: What else could Hemant do to check whether the work fits his goal, and why?
qa.a: He could ask someone who works in coding which skills matter, because it shows whether these jobs are building the right abilities.

qa.q: How might the tuition teacher see Hemant's message?
qa.a: The tuition teacher may see a keen, reliable student who wants to grow his skills, and also gains help with another site.

grounding: After three months a student asks whether the gig builds skills for a career, keeps the coding jobs and drops the least useful.

passage:
“Why are you glaring at a spreadsheet?” Didi asked, leaning on Leela's door.
“I'm adding. School, seven hours, five days: thirty-five. Three coaching batches: twelve. Bus rides: eight. Homework: seven.”
“And sleep?”
“It's not on the sheet.” Leela's voice cracked. “Didi, it's sixty-two hours. Sixty-two, and I still fall behind. I keep telling myself I'm just not trying hard enough.”
Didi sat on the bed and took the pencil. “Sixty-two hours a week, before eating and before any rest. Who could try hard enough for that?”
“So it's not me?”
“It's the total. You're carrying a full-time job and calling yourself lazy.”
Leela laughed shakily and wiped her eyes. “Then what do I change?”
“Tomorrow we look at what each batch actually gives you.”

qa.q: How many hours a week did Leela's tally come to?
qa.a: Sixty-two hours.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling about herself before adding it up?
qa.a: Guilt and self-doubt: she kept telling herself she was not trying hard enough.

qa.q: What could Leela do next with the total, and why?
qa.a: She could compare what each batch adds and trim or move the least useful one, because the problem is the total load, not her effort.

qa.q: How does Didi see Leela's problem?
qa.a: Didi sees a younger sister blaming herself for a timetable that would exhaust anyone, and wants her to see the load as the real problem.

grounding: A student adds up school, coaching, travel and homework, and sees that the problem is total load, not lack of effort.

subtype: Approach: prioritising the classes that add most [Action]
passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Pradeep (Class 11) came in with a sheet listing his coaching batches in two columns: “explains new ideas” and “repeats what school already did”. The physics problem-solving batch and the chemistry doubts class went in the first column; the maths revision batch went in the second. He said he had been awake past one every night. I asked what he wanted to do. He chose to keep the first two and drop maths revision, then planned to use the freed evenings for solving his own problems and going to bed earlier. I asked how he would know it worked; he suggested comparing test scores after a month. I have asked his parents to come in on the 14th so we can review it together. — Rafiq

qa.q: Which batch did Pradeep drop?
qa.a: The maths revision batch, which repeated what school had covered.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel about cutting a batch?
qa.a: Cautious relief: he chose deliberately and wanted to test the change with scores, showing some worry but mostly a sense of relief after losing sleep.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do if scores dip after the change, and why?
qa.a: He could review the results with Rafiq and add one batch back or use the freed time for more practice, since a choice made with evidence can be adjusted.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's parents see the change?
qa.a: They may worry that fewer classes means falling behind, so the review on the 14th and the score comparison give them evidence to judge whether it works.

grounding: A student compares which batches clarify concepts and which repeat school content, keeps the two that help and uses the freed time for self-study and sleep.
